Jacques Tati. A French filmmaker, actor, and mime who created a singular comedy of observation, using elaborately designed sets and silent-film timing to expose the absurdities of modern life and technological progress. His character Monsieur Hulot became cinema's great comic archetype of the man perpetually at odds with an increasingly sterile, automated world.

He created and played Monsieur Hulot, a bowlegged, pipe-smoking protagonist whose bemused incompetence with modern machinery drives films exploring mid-century modernism's human cost. He directed Playtime in 1967, an audacious live-action cartoon set in a vast mock-modern Paris built on soundstages—shot in seventy millimetre and a one-to-one-point-sixty-six ratio, a technical marvel and a financial disaster. My Uncle in 1958 contrasts the cluttered, organic chaos of a working-class neighbourhood with the antiseptic sterility of a modernist villa and its labour-saving gimmicks.

Tati worked primarily in comedy without dialogue, or with barely audible mumbling and sound effects, returning cinema to the silent tradition of Chaplin and Keaton. He filmed in long takes and wide shots, allowing the viewer to scan the frame and discover gags independently. His compositions are dense with simultaneous action. His films took years to complete due to meticulously designed sets and locations. Playtime was in production for over a decade. He remained adamantly auteurist, refusing studio interference and maintaining total control over form and meaning.

He shares with Charles Chaplin the tradition of silent comedy and its philosophy. Buster Keaton was another influence in physical comedy and compositional sophistication. He was a contemporary New Wave radical with Jean-Luc Godard, both rejecting conventional narrative. His work is a critique of nineteen-fifties to nineteen-sixties design and modernism lifestyle.
